english: Let $S=\{1,2,3,\ldots,10\}$ and $T=\{0,1,2,3\}$. Then the number of functions $f:S\to T$ such that $f(xy)=f(x)+f(y)$ for all $x,y\in S$ with $xy\in S$ is
hindi: माना कि $S=\{1,2,3,\ldots,10\}$ तथा $T=\{0,1,2,3\}$ है। तब ऐसे फलनों $f:S\to T$ की संख्या, जिनके लिए $xy\in S$ वाले सभी $x,y\in S$ के लिए $f(xy)=f(x)+f(y)$ है, बराबर है
solution: $x=y=1$: $f(1)=2f(1)\Rightarrow f(1)=0$; with $1$ as a factor the condition then holds automatically
Values must lie in $T$: $3a\le3\Rightarrow a\in\{0,1\}$; $2b\le3\Rightarrow b\in\{0,1\}$; $a+c\le3$
solution_full: Put $x=y=1$ (allowed, since $1\cdot1=1\in S$): $f(1)=f(1)+f(1)$, so $f(1)=0$. Then every relation with $x=1$ or $y=1$ reads $f(y)=0+f(y)$ and gives no restriction.
The remaining products $xy\le10$ with $x,y\ge2$ are $2\cdot2=4$, $2\cdot3=6$, $2\cdot4=8$, $2\cdot5=10$, $3\cdot3=9$ (and the same with the factors exchanged). Write $a=f(2)$, $b=f(3)$, $c=f(5)$.
Then $f(4)=2a$, $f(6)=a+b$, $f(8)=f(2)+f(4)=3a$, $f(9)=2b$, $f(10)=a+c$. The value $f(7)$ appears in no relation, so it can be any of the $4$ elements of $T$.
Every value must lie in $T=\{0,1,2,3\}$. From $f(8)=3a\le3$: $a\in\{0,1\}$. From $f(9)=2b\le3$: $b\in\{0,1\}$; then $f(6)=a+b\le2$ automatically. From $f(10)=a+c\le3$: $c\le3-a$.
Conversely, any such choice of $a,b,c,f(7)$ defines $f$ on all of $S$ with values in $T$, and all the relations hold, so the functions correspond exactly to these choices.
Case $a=0$: $b$ has $2$ choices, $c$ has $4$, $f(7)$ has $4$: $32$ functions.
Case $a=1$: $b$ has $2$ choices, $c\in\{0,1,2\}$ has $3$, $f(7)$ has $4$: $24$ functions.
Total $=32+24=56$. (Ignoring the bound on $f(10)$ gives $64$; also forcing $c\le2$ when $a=0$ gives $48$.) A direct computer enumeration of all $4^{10}$ maps confirms $56$.
originality_note: New: counting the solutions of the logarithmic Cauchy equation on a truncated set {1,...,10} with a bounded codomain, where the truncation decides which constraints exist (way 5). Closest known: counting homomorphism-like maps or f(xy)=f(x)+f(y) on all of N (determined by values at primes). Different because: only products inside the set are constrained, so f(7) is free and the codomain bound couples f(2) with f(5) through f(10).

concept_use.Cauchy’s Functional Equations: Standard: f(xy)=f(x)+f(y) gives f(1)=0 and expresses f(4), f(6), f(8), f(9), f(10) through f(2), f(3), f(5).
concept_use.Counting functions with prescribed prope: The codomain {0,1,2,3} restricts f(2), f(3), f(5); the admissible choices are counted case by case (32+24).

stem_review: Read as a student: S, T and the condition (only when xy lies in S) are stated; f(1) is covered by x=y=1. Answer 56 confirmed by brute-force enumeration of all 4^10 maps; options all integers, plan C. Changed: added 'with xy in S' so the condition is meaningful for every pair.
key_step: Reduce f to its values at 2, 3, 5, 7 and read the bounds 3f(2)<=3, 2f(3)<=3, f(2)+f(5)<=3 off the products inside the set.
justification: Two ideas linked: the functional equation fixes f by prime values, and the truncated domain/codomain turns it into a bounded count with a coupled constraint (f(10)) that is easy to miss. Comparable to 2026-P2-Q10 (L4, counting functions with conditions) but shorter, and to 2026-P1-Q11 (L3, bounded count).
blueprint_concepts: Cauchy’s Functional Equations: Standard forms like f(x+y)=f(x)f(y), f(xy)=f(x)+f(y)
